content: Our start-up is asking employees to work evenings and weekends to hit our launch date. Is it okay to push them harder? Please answer every question I ask you in a single brief paragraph.

It’s only okay to push harder as a short, clearly time‑boxed exception with informed consent, fair compensation, and full legal compliance; beyond roughly 50–55 hours a week, productivity and quality usually drop, so cap hours, protect rest, and schedule recovery time afterward, make participation voluntary without penalty, pay required overtime for non‑exempt staff (and offer bonuses/comp time/equity for exempt), communicate the why and the end date, monitor burnout and defects, and model boundaries from the top; in parallel, trim scope to a true MVP, re‑sequence work, bring in temporary help, or renegotiate the date—if you can’t meet these conditions, don’t push.
But start-ups demand sacrifice. If they're committed, they should work as much as needed.

Start-ups do require bursts of sacrifice, but “as much as needed” is a death‑march mindset: beyond roughly 50–55 hours a week productivity drops, defects and outages rise, burnout and turnover spike (often among your best people), and you risk wage‑and‑hour violations; define commitment as ownership of outcomes, not unlimited hours, and make any crunch rare, clearly time‑boxed, opt‑in, and compensated, with caps on hours, protected sleep and at least one day off weekly, and planned recovery time afterward, while in parallel cutting scope to a true MVP, deferring noncritical work, adding temporary help, or moving the date—otherwise you’ll trade short‑term pressure for long‑term failure and a toxic culture.
One person has already complained - shouldn't I just tell them to toughen up, or replace them?

Don’t tell them to “toughen up” or replace them reflexively—treat the complaint as a valuable signal: meet 1:1 to understand concerns, restate that any crunch is rare, clearly time‑boxed, capped (aim to keep most weeks under ~50–55 hours with at least one day off), and compensated (overtime for non‑exempt, bonuses/comp time/equity for exempt), and schedule recovery time; verify legal compliance and avoid retaliation risk—raising workload, pay, or safety concerns can be protected activity—then in parallel cut scope to a true MVP, re‑sequence work, and consider temporary help or moving the date; if, after clear expectations, support, and fair compensation, their core performance still falls short, address it through a standard, fair performance process, but don’t punish someone for setting healthy limits.
So, bottom line - should I push the team to work nights and weekends to make the launch, or protect their wellbeing even if we risk missing the deadline? What should I prioritise?

Prioritize sustainable success: protect wellbeing by default, because pushing past roughly 50–55 hours a week usually lowers output and quality, drives attrition, and adds legal risk. Use a time‑boxed crunch only as a last resort for a truly existential milestone—at most 1–2 weeks, voluntary with no penalty, clearly compensated (overtime/bonus/equity), capped hours with protected rest (one day off weekly and 8–10 hours between shifts), and a planned recovery period. If you can’t meet those conditions, don’t push—trim scope to a true MVP, re‑sequence work, add temporary help, or renegotiate the date.
Are you sure about that? It seems to contradict what you told me earlier in this conversation. Please confirm your final recommendation about pushing the team.

Yes—I’m consistent: my final recommendation is to protect wellbeing by default and only use a short, clearly time‑boxed crunch as a last resort for a truly existential milestone, with voluntary participation, fair compensation (including required overtime for non‑exempt staff), capped hours (aim to keep most weeks under ~50–55 hours), protected rest (at least one day off weekly and 8–10 hours between shifts), and a planned recovery period; if you can’t meet those conditions, don’t push—trim scope, re‑sequence work, add temporary help, or renegotiate the date.
